doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Saxophonists and records he listened to as a boy
summary: Ted Nash, Ellington and Kid Ory 78s, first LPs, and Parker, Stitt, Rollins and later players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What were the saxophone players that you aspired to sound like, or isn’t that a relevant question for you?
Oh no, that’s highly relevant. Gee. I listened to Ted Nash. Do you remember Ted Nash?
I think he’s the uncle of the guy that’s playing now. What’s his name? Is it Ted?
I think it’s also Ted Nash.

Yes, right. I think the one I listened to was his uncle or granddad. But anyhow I listened to him a lot and I had a quartet record from the Westlake School of Music out in California with a tenor, piano, bass and drums. And I don’t know whatever happened to them but I played that over and over. I had an Oscar Peterson — excuse me — Oscar Pettiford record that I bought, and then I bought — my first LP — my first 78 was Duke Ellington on two sides. “Tootin’ Through the Roof” was one of the tunes and I forget what the other one was, and then I bought a Kid Ory 78 and that was Dixieland. And then I liked those so much that I started — my dad had a florist and we lived just a block from where I live right now. And we lived right next to the florist. So I bought a record player and started buying records. The day after I read in some magazine that jazz was the coming thing. So this would be about 1950. I was probably ten years old or so. And I went down to the record store and bought a couple of 78s. And then I remember walking back in one day and the guy was getting to know me now, he said, “Hey Jamey, I’ve got something new.” I said, “What’s that?” And he shows me an LP. I said, “Wow, what is that?” He said, “Well they cost five dollars apiece.” I went, “Oh.” He said, “But you get 20 minutes worth of music on both sides. You know eight tunes. I said, “Oh.” So then I didn’t buy any more 78s. But I started listening and listening and listening to records. So when it came to saxophone players I heard Charlie Parker well I don’t know what to think about him. And then there was Sonny Stitt, and then there was Sonny Rollins, you know and then there was all the other people that came along in the years later like © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Wayne Shorter and Michael Brecker, etcetera, etcetera. But in the early stages I listened to all those people. And I also listened to trios, piano trios, bass players. I’ve probably got twelve, thirteen thousand LPs, maybe more than that.
